The Passive: The Present Continuous and Present Perfect Tenses

You use the Present Continuous to talk about an action that is happening at the time of speaking. The action or event is in progress.
They're being a little hot-headed.

You use the Present Perfect to talk about a finished action or event with present consequences. There is a connection between what happened in the past and the present.
The wind has moved the air for eons.
You often choose the passive form when you want to talk about an action but are not so interested in saying who or what does/did it. Passives without agents (the doers) are common in storytelling.
Look at the chart below for the structure of the passive voice.

Reported Speech and Questions

You use reported speech (indirect speech) when you are saying (reporting) what other people said.
This style of writing is common in storytelling. It allows the writer to share dialogue with the reader without always using quotation marks.

When you tell people what someone has said you generally make the verb tense 'more in the past' since we are reporting the information at a later time. You need to change the verb to the next past form.
For example:

You have to change the pronoun if you are reporting what someone else said. Compare these two sentences. In each case the person actually said "I don't want to go."

• I said, “I don't want to go.” > I said I didn't want to go.
  • Bill said, “I don't want to go.” > Bill said he didn't want to go.
When you want to report questions asked, the subject normally comes before the verb.

Direct: Where is the sun?
Indirect: The wind asked where the sun was.
When the question is a yes/no question, you use if or whether to report it.
The sun asks if/whether the wind would be around without shifting temperatures.

images.text:
So here's an old myth. It's vaguely based on a fable by Aesop, the Roman storyteller who told tales with morals attached. It's kind of fun!

The wind and the sun are talking. They're being a little hot-headed. The air has been moved by the wind for eons. The Earth has been warmed by the sun for endless time. Now, the question of who is actually stronger is being discussed.

The sun asks if the wind would be around without shifting temperatures. The wind retorts that without a cooling breeze, the Earth would certainly burn. After polite insults have been exchanged, they notice a traveler coming down the road. The sun suggests that having a test subject would be just the ticket. The wind queries whether anyone would ever agree with the sun.

A cloak has been draped over the traveler's shoulders. The sun says that whichever of them makes the traveller take off his cloak is the stronger of the two. The wind accepts the challenge.

Then, the sun is being directed to hide while the wind struts his stuff. He blows as hard as he can but the traveler isn't being persuaded to remove his cloak. The wind asks himself why the traveller was wrapping his cloak around himself even tighter. Finally the wind gives up. The sun comes gliding out. He shines down upon the traveller, who soon finds it hot, then takes off his cloak.

The sun, beaming at the wind, says he had always known that gentle persuasion was better than force.
